title: Nutrition and digestion
intro: What's in your food and what happens to it after you swallow? Learn the nutrients in a balanced diet and the journey through the digestive system.
description: Free KS3 Biology questions with answers on nutrition and digestion: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water, a balanced diet, the digestive system and enzymes. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9.

questions.q: Which nutrient is the body's main source of energy?
questions.hint: Bread, pasta and rice are full of it.
questions.explain: Carbohydrates, such as starch and sugars, are the main source of energy.

questions.q: Which nutrient is needed for growth and repair?
questions.hint: Meat, fish, eggs, beans and lentils are rich in it.
questions.explain: Protein is used to build and repair cells, for example muscle.

options: It helps food move through the gut
questions.hint: It's in vegetables, fruit and wholegrain bread.
questions.explain: Fibre isn't digested, but it helps food move through the intestines and prevents constipation.

questions.q: Which mineral do bones and teeth need?
questions.hint: Milk and cheese are good sources.
questions.explain: Calcium is needed for strong bones and teeth. Iron is needed for red blood cells.

questions.q: Sailors long ago got a disease called scurvy because they ate no fresh fruit. Which vitamin were they missing?
questions.hint: Oranges and lemons are full of it.
questions.explain: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C. Sailors were given citrus fruit to prevent it.

options: Eating the right amount of each nutrient
Eating the same amount of every food
questions.hint: Too much or too little of anything can be a problem.
questions.explain: A balanced diet has the right amounts of each nutrient. Some fat is needed too: it stores energy and keeps you warm.
Digestion starts in the mouth: teeth break food into smaller pieces and saliva starts to digest starch.

questions.q: Which is the right order for food to travel through the body?
options: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine
Mouth → stomach → oesophagus → large intestine → small intestine
Mouth → small intestine → stomach → large intestine
questions.hint: The oesophagus is the tube from your mouth to your stomach.
questions.explain: Mouth, oesophagus (food pipe), stomach, small intestine, large intestine, then out through the rectum and anus.

questions.q: Where are most digested nutrients absorbed into the blood?
questions.hint: It's long and folded, with a huge surface area.
questions.explain: Nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine. Its walls are covered in tiny finger-like villi that give it a big surface area.

questions.q: What is the main job of the large intestine?
options: To absorb water from undigested food
questions.hint: What's left after the small intestine has taken the nutrients?
questions.explain: The large intestine absorbs water. What's left is stored in the rectum and leaves through the anus as faeces.

questions.q: Why does the stomach contain acid?
options: It kills bacteria and helps enzymes work
questions.hint: Food isn't always free of germs.
questions.explain: Stomach acid kills most bacteria in food, and the stomach's enzymes work best in acid.

options: Break large food molecules into small ones the body can absorb
questions.hint: Small molecules can pass into the blood.
questions.explain: Enzymes are biological catalysts. Digestive enzymes break big molecules like starch and protein into small ones that can be absorbed.

questions.q: Saliva contains an enzyme called amylase. What does it break down?
questions.hint: Chew bread for a long time and it starts to taste sweet.
questions.explain: Amylase breaks starch into sugars. That's why bread tastes sweeter if you chew it for a while.

questions.q: Iodine solution is added to a food and turns blue-black. What does the food contain?
questions.hint: The iodine test is for one nutrient.
questions.explain: Iodine turns from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present.
